lessons.description: The organs that produce digestive enzymes, and the conditions they need to work.
keyPoints: Digestive enzymes break down large, insoluble food molecules into smaller, soluble ones that can be absorbed.
Carbohydrases break carbohydrates down into simple sugars, and amylase breaks starch down into maltose.
Maltase breaks down maltose into glucose.
Proteases break down proteins into amino acids.
Lipases break down lipids into glycerol and fatty acids.
The pancreas and small intestine produce all three main types of digestive enzyme.
The stomach produces hydrochloric acid to kill bacteria and provide the acidic conditions its protease needs.
Bile is produced in the liver and stored in the gall bladder.
Bile neutralises stomach acid and emulsifies fats to give lipase a larger surface area to act on.

lessons.description: The three types of neurone, their structure, and how they are adapted to carry electrical impulses quickly.
keyPoints: Receptors detect a stimulus, and effectors, which are muscles or glands, carry out the response.
The central nervous system coordinates a response by receiving information from sensory neurones and sending impulses out along motor neurones.
Neurones are adapted to carry electrical impulses quickly by being very long and having an insulating myelin sheath.
A nerve signal crosses a synapse when a neurotransmitter diffuses across the gap and sets off a new electrical impulse.
Reflex actions are rapid and automatic because they happen without any conscious thought.
In a reflex arc, the electrical impulse passes through a relay neurone in the spinal cord or an unconscious part of the brain.

lessons.description: The hierarchy of cells, tissues, organs and organ systems that make up a multicellular organism.
keyPoints: Cells in a multicellular organism are arranged into a hierarchy of increasingly complex levels.
The levels of organisation, from simplest to most complex, are cell, tissue, organ, organ system and organism.
Sub-cellular structures, such as the nucleus and mitochondria, sit below the cellular level.

lessons.description: The medical dangers of stem cell therapies and the moral debates surrounding the use of human embryos.
keyPoints: Adult stem cells from bone marrow can be transplanted to treat blood conditions like leukaemia.
Embryonic stem cells can be made to differentiate into any type of cell to replace damaged tissues.
Stem cell transplants carry risks such as viral contamination, tumour formation and rejection.
Using embryonic stem cells is controversial because the embryos are destroyed to harvest the cells.

lessons.description: The repeating sequence of growth, DNA duplication and division that a cell goes through.
keyPoints: Mitosis is a type of cell division that produces two genetically identical diploid daughter cells.
Multicellular organisms use mitosis to grow and to replace damaged cells.
Before a cell divides, it goes through interphase to grow and duplicate its DNA.
During mitosis, the chromosomes line up and cell fibres pull the two copies of each chromosome to opposite ends of the cell.

lessons.description: How breathing rate and heart rate increase to supply working muscles with more oxygen and glucose.
keyPoints: During exercise, muscles need more energy from respiration so they require more oxygen and glucose.
Heart rate and breathing rate increase during exercise to supply the active muscles with oxygen and glucose faster.
During very vigorous exercise, the body cannot deliver oxygen fast enough and muscles begin to respire anaerobically as well.
The incomplete oxidation of glucose makes lactic acid build up in the muscles, which creates an oxygen debt.
Anaerobic respiration produces lactic acid and can cause muscles to become fatigued over a long period.

lessons.description: How waves of muscle contraction push balls of food along the gut.
keyPoints: Food travels in one direction along the alimentary canal, passing through organs that each have a specific job.
Peristalsis is a wave of muscle contraction and relaxation that pushes food along the gut.
Villi and microvilli give the small intestine a very large surface area for fast absorption.
A wall one cell thick and a rich blood supply help the villus absorb products quickly.
Fatty acids and glycerol are absorbed into the lacteal and transported in lymph before entering the blood.

lessons.description: The mechanisms the skin and muscles use to cool the body down or warm it back up.
keyPoints: The body maintains a core temperature of about 37 °C as this is the optimum temperature for its enzymes.
The thermoregulatory centre in the brain monitors blood temperature and receives nervous impulses from skin receptors.
Sweating cools the body because energy is transferred to the environment as the water evaporates.
Vasodilation widens the blood vessels supplying the skin, so more blood flows near the surface and more heat is lost to the surroundings.
Vasoconstriction narrows the blood vessels supplying the skin, so less blood flows near the surface and less heat is lost to the surroundings.
Shivering warms the body because the extra muscle contraction requires respiration, which releases energy.

lessons.h1: 10.4 - Effect of pH, Temperature & Concentration on Enzyme Activity
lessons.description: Turning digestion times into rates, plotting rate against pH, and finding the optimum pH from the peak.
How interconnected food chains form a network, and why populations are interdependent.
keyPoints: Every food chain begins with a producer that makes glucose by photosynthesis.
Arrows in a food chain point in the direction of energy transfer, from the organism eaten to the one that eats it.
The amount of energy and biomass available falls at each step up a food chain.
A food web shows how individual food chains overlap and interconnect in a community.
Organisms in a food web are interdependent, so a change in one population has knock-on effects on the others.

lessons.description: Why large areas of forest are cleared, and the consequences for the atmosphere, soil and biodiversity.
keyPoints: Forests are often cleared to provide land for cattle, crops or biofuels.
Deforestation increases carbon dioxide in the atmosphere because there are fewer trees to photosynthesise.
Burning cleared forests releases the carbon stored in the trees as carbon dioxide.
Removing tree cover leads to soil erosion, leaching and a disturbed water cycle.
Destroying a forest habitat sharply reduces biodiversity and can drive species to extinction.

lessons.description: The organs involved in female reproduction and how they prepare for a potential pregnancy.
keyPoints: Puberty is triggered by reproductive hormones and causes the development of secondary sexual characteristics.
Testosterone is produced by the testes and stimulates sperm production.
Oestrogen is produced by the ovaries and causes female secondary sexual characteristics to develop.
The menstrual cycle is a monthly sequence that releases an egg and prepares the uterus lining for a fertilised egg.
Ovulation is the release of an egg from an ovary, which usually happens around day 14 of the cycle.
If an egg is not fertilised, progesterone levels fall and the uterus lining breaks down during menstruation.
FSH causes an egg to mature in the ovary, and LH triggers the release of the egg.
Oestrogen causes the uterus lining to build up, and progesterone maintains this thickened lining.
Oestrogen inhibits FSH and stimulates LH, while progesterone inhibits both FSH and LH to prevent more eggs maturing.

lessons.description: How to calculate the percentage of biomass passed from one trophic level to the next.
keyPoints: Only about 10% of the biomass at one trophic level is passed on to the level above.
Biomass is lost because not all food is eaten, not all is absorbed, and much is used in respiration.
Food chains rarely have more than five trophic levels because too little energy is left to support another level.
The efficiency of biomass transfer is the percentage of biomass passed on to the next trophic level.
A pyramid of biomass uses horizontal bars to show the total mass of organisms at each trophic level.
A pyramid of biomass is almost always a true pyramid shape because biomass is lost at every transfer.
A pyramid of number shows the count of organisms, which can create an irregular shape if organisms vary greatly in size.
A pyramid of energy shows the rate of energy transfer and is always a true upright pyramid because energy decreases up the chain.

lessons.description: How cells use oxygen to fully break down glucose and release a large amount of energy.
keyPoints: Respiration is an exothermic reaction that happens continuously in all living cells to release energy from glucose.
Aerobic respiration uses oxygen to fully break down glucose into carbon dioxide and water.
Aerobic respiration transfers far more energy per glucose molecule than anaerobic respiration.
Anaerobic respiration partially breaks down glucose without using oxygen.
Anaerobic respiration in animal cells produces lactic acid.
Anaerobic respiration in yeast and plant cells produces ethanol and carbon dioxide.

lessons.description: How to test a sample for reducing sugars and estimate their concentration.
keyPoints: Iodine solution changes from yellow-brown to blue-black when starch is present.
Benedict's solution changes from blue to a green, yellow, orange or brick-red precipitate when heated with a reducing sugar.
Biuret reagent changes from blue to purple when protein is present.
Sudan III stain separates a mixture into two layers, turning the top layer bright red if lipids are present.

lessons.description: The potential dangers of genetic modification to the environment, food chains and human health.
keyPoints: Genetically modifying crops to resist insects reduces crop damage and the need for pesticides.
Crops made tolerant to herbicides allow farmers to kill weeds without harming the crop itself.
Transplanted genes could escape into the wild and create weeds that are resistant to weedkiller.
Growing GM crops can reduce farmland biodiversity and affect local food chains.

lessons.description: How the body maintains a constant internal environment, and the three parts of an automatic control system.
keyPoints: Homeostasis keeps conditions inside the body steady so that cells and enzymes can function properly.
Body temperature, blood glucose concentration and water content are all controlled by automatic systems.
An automatic control system consists of receptors, a coordination centre and effectors.

lessons.description: The pros and cons of sexual and asexual reproduction, and how variation and speed affect survival.
keyPoints: Sexual reproduction produces variation in offspring because they inherit a mixture of genes from two parents.
Variation gives a population a survival advantage if the environment changes or a disease breaks out.
Sexual reproduction takes more time and energy than asexual reproduction, and requires finding a mate.
Asexual reproduction needs only one parent, making it faster and more energy-efficient than sexual reproduction.
Asexual reproduction produces genetically identical offspring, so a whole population can be affected by a single disease.
In crop production, asexual reproduction produces a uniform yield and allows plants to be harvested sooner.

lessons.description: The lifestyle and fixed factors that increase the chance of developing coronary heart disease.
keyPoints: Coronary heart disease occurs when fatty deposits build up and block the coronary arteries, starving the heart muscle of oxygen.
Lifestyle risk factors for cardiovascular disease include smoking, a lack of exercise, and a diet high in salt and saturated fat.

lessons.description: How to observe osmosis by measuring the change in mass of potato cylinders in different sugar solutions.
keyPoints: Osmosis is the net flow of water across a partially permeable membrane from a region of higher water concentration to a lower one.
A partially permeable membrane has small holes that let tiny molecules like water pass through, but block larger ones.
A potato cylinder gains mass in a dilute solution as water moves in, and loses mass in a concentrated solution as water moves out.

lessons.description: What xylem transports, the direction of flow, and where it is found in the plant.
keyPoints: Xylem tissue transports water and dissolved mineral ions upwards from the roots to the leaves.
Phloem tissue transports dissolved sugars and amino acids in both directions around the plant.
Xylem is found near the outside of a stem, in the centre of a root, and in the veins of a leaf.
Translocation is the movement of sugars and amino acids through the phloem.
Root hair cells have a very large surface area to absorb water and mineral ions quickly.
Plants absorb water by osmosis and mineral ions by active transport.
Water travels from root hair cells through the root cortex, up the xylem and into the mesophyll cells of the leaf.

lessons.description: The stages of transferring a gene using restriction enzymes, ligase, and a vector.
keyPoints: Genetic engineering changes an organism's genome by adding a gene taken from a different organism.
A restriction enzyme cuts the DNA to leave sticky ends, and ligase joins complementary sticky ends together.
Bacteria can be genetically modified to produce large amounts of human insulin to treat diabetes.
Crops can be genetically modified to resist herbicides or insect pests, which increases their yield.

lessons.description: The main glands of the endocrine system and the specific chemical messengers they release.
keyPoints: Hormones are chemical messengers made by endocrine glands and carried in the blood.
A hormone only affects target cells that have specific receptor proteins shaped to fit it.
The pituitary gland acts as a master gland, releasing hormones that trigger other glands to secrete their own hormones.
The thyroid gland secretes thyroxine to regulate the body's metabolic rate.
The pancreas secretes insulin and glucagon to regulate blood glucose levels.
The adrenal glands secrete adrenaline to prepare the body for a fight-or-flight response.
The ovaries and testes secrete hormones involved in reproduction.
The nervous system uses very fast, short-lived electrical impulses to target precise areas.
The endocrine system uses slower, long-lasting chemical messengers that act widely across the body.

lessons.description: How to use a family tree to find parents' genotypes and predict the chance of their next child inheriting a disorder.
keyPoints: A family pedigree is a chart that shows how a characteristic is passed down through the generations of a family.
In a pedigree diagram, squares represent males, circles represent females, and shaded shapes represent people who have the characteristic.
A person with an inherited recessive disorder must have a homozygous recessive genotype.
If two unaffected parents have a child with a recessive disorder, both parents must be heterozygous carriers.
Characteristics caused by a dominant allele have no carriers because a single copy is enough to show the trait.
You can predict the chance of a child inheriting a disorder by reading the parents' genotypes from a pedigree and doing a genetic cross.
The probability of inheriting a disorder is a separate, independent event for every child a couple has.

lessons.description: How lymphocytes produce antibodies that bind to specific antigens on the surface of pathogens.
keyPoints: Phagocytes are white blood cells that track down, engulf and destroy pathogens.
Lymphocytes are white blood cells that produce antibodies with a complementary shape to a specific antigen.

lessons.description: Where stem cells are found in animals, and the range of cell types they can turn into.
keyPoints: Stem cells can either divide to produce more stem cells, or develop into specialised cells like nerve or muscle cells.
Stem cells are the source of the new specialised cells an organism needs as it grows and develops, and of the new cells that replace worn-out or damaged ones.
Embryonic stem cells are found in early embryos and can develop into any kind of cell in the body.
Adult stem cells are found in places like bone marrow and can only develop into a limited range of cell types.
Adult stem cells are used to replace damaged or worn out cells for growth and repair.

lessons.description: Using the magnification formula to find image size, actual size, and magnification.
keyPoints: Magnification is calculated by dividing the image size by the actual size.
Image size and actual size must be converted to the same unit before calculating magnification.
There are 1,000 micrometres in a millimetre, and 1,000 nanometres in a micrometre.
To convert millimetres to micrometres, multiply by 1,000.

lessons.description: Why the body must balance its water content, and how the kidneys adjust water loss.
keyPoints: The kidneys are the main organs of excretion and remove urea, excess water and excess ions from the blood.
The water content of the blood must be kept steady so that cells do not gain or lose too much water by osmosis.
The kidneys filter the blood and then reabsorb useful substances and a controlled amount of water.
The pituitary gland releases more ADH when the blood is too concentrated, causing the kidneys to reabsorb more water.

lessons.description: The difference between characteristics that fall into distinct categories and those that range between two extremes.
keyPoints: Differences between individuals of a species are caused by their genes, their environment, or a combination of both.
New genetic variation originally arises from mutations that create new alleles.
Most characteristics are determined by a mixture of genetic and environmental factors.
Characteristics showing continuous variation can take any value within a range and are caused by both genes and the environment.
Characteristics showing discontinuous variation fall into distinct categories and are usually controlled by a single gene.

lessons.description: How to read rate graphs to identify which environmental factor is holding back photosynthesis.
keyPoints: Increasing a limiting factor raises the rate of photosynthesis, but increasing any other factor makes no difference.
The rate of photosynthesis increases with temperature up to an optimum, then falls to zero as enzymes are denatured.
A shortage of chlorophyll reduces the rate of photosynthesis because the plant cannot absorb as much light.
On a rate graph, the factor on the horizontal axis is the limiting factor where the line is rising.
Where a line on a rate graph levels off, a different factor has become the limiting factor.

lessons.description: How humans pollute water, air and land with waste and harmful chemicals, and how this harms organisms and reduces biodiversity.
keyPoints: High biodiversity makes ecosystems more stable because species have other feeding relationships to fall back on if one species declines.
Human activities like using up resources, destroying habitats and producing waste are reducing biodiversity.
Pollution on land, in water and in the air kills plants and animals, which reduces biodiversity.
Carbon monoxide from burning fuels binds to haemoglobin in red blood cells and reduces the amount of oxygen the blood can carry.

lessons.description: How light intensity, temperature, humidity, wind speed and surface area change the speed of water loss.
keyPoints: Transpiration is the loss of water vapour from a plant, mostly by evaporation and diffusion from the leaves.
Water lost from the leaves draws more water up from the roots through the xylem in a continuous flow called the transpiration stream.
Higher temperatures increase the rate of transpiration because water molecules have more energy to evaporate and diffuse out of the leaf.
Higher wind speeds increase the rate of transpiration by sweeping away water vapour and keeping the concentration outside the leaf low.
Higher humidity decreases the rate of transpiration because there is a smaller difference in water concentration between the inside and outside of the leaf.
Brighter light increases the rate of transpiration because the stomata open to let in carbon dioxide for photosynthesis.

lessons.description: Turning lamp distances into relative light intensities with 1/d^^2^^, and seeing that the rate follows the light intensity, not the distance.
Calculating and comparing the surface area to volume ratios of two differently sized animals.
keyPoints: Volume increases faster than surface area as an object grows, so larger organisms have a smaller surface area to volume ratio.
A large surface area compared with the volume and a short diffusion distance make the exchange of substances easy.
Single-celled organisms have a large surface area to volume ratio, allowing them to rely on simple diffusion to supply their whole volume.
Large multicellular organisms have a small surface area to volume ratio, so diffusion across their outer surface alone is too slow.
Large organisms need specialised exchange surfaces to exchange substances efficiently with their environment.
Large organisms need a transport system to carry substances between their exchange surfaces and the rest of their cells.

lessons.description: How plants use glucose for respiration and convert it into cellulose, starch, and other useful substances.
keyPoints: Photosynthesis is an endothermic reaction that uses light energy to convert carbon dioxide and water into glucose and oxygen.
Plants use the glucose they make for respiration, or convert it into other useful substances like insoluble starch for storage.
Gases move in and out of the leaf through small pores called stomata.
Net gas exchange depends on light intensity, with plants taking in carbon dioxide overall only in bright light.
At the compensation point, the rates of photosynthesis and respiration are equal, so there is no net gas exchange.

lessons.description: Finding the mean number of daisies per quadrat and scaling it up to estimate the population of a whole field.
Why the amount of energy a person needs from their food depends on their activity level, age and whether they are pregnant.
keyPoints: A balanced diet supplies all the essential nutrients the body needs in the right proportions.
Carbohydrates provide energy, lipids store energy, and proteins are needed for growth and repair.
Energy needs increase with higher activity levels and during childhood and teenage years.
A pregnant woman needs more energy from her food to supply the developing baby.

lessons.description: Why the random shuffling of chromosome pairs means every gamete is genetically unique.
keyPoints: Meiosis is a type of cell division that produces four haploid gametes from one diploid cell.
Before meiosis begins, the cell duplicates its DNA so each chromosome forms an X shape.
Meiosis involves two cell divisions, one straight after the other.
Fertilisation restores the full diploid number of chromosomes by joining two haploid gametes.
During meiosis, chromosome pairs are pulled apart so each new cell gets a random mixture of the mother's and father's chromosomes.
Because the chromosomes are randomly shuffled, every gamete produced by meiosis is genetically different.
Mitosis produces two identical diploid cells, whereas meiosis produces four varied haploid cells.

lessons.description: How the eye changes the shape of its lens to focus on objects at different distances.
keyPoints: To focus on a near object, the ciliary muscle contracts and the lens becomes fatter to refract light more strongly.
To focus on a distant object, the ciliary muscle relaxes and the lens becomes thinner to refract light less.

lessons.description: The human activities that release carbon dioxide, methane, nitrous oxide and CFCs into the atmosphere.
keyPoints: Greenhouse gases absorb outgoing energy and re-radiate it to keep the Earth warm.
Carbon dioxide, methane, water vapour, nitrous oxide and CFCs act as greenhouse gases.
The enhanced greenhouse effect traps more heat and causes the Earth's temperature to rise.
Human activities like burning fossil fuels and deforestation release carbon dioxide.
Rearing cattle and growing rice in flooded paddies release methane.
Changing temperatures and rainfall patterns cause the distribution of many species to shift.
Higher temperatures cause seawater to expand and ice caps to melt, leading to rising sea levels.
Biodiversity falls because some species cannot adapt or migrate quickly enough to survive the climate changes.

lessons.description: How vaccines introduce antigens to stimulate lymphocytes to produce antibodies and memory cells.
keyPoints: A vaccine contains a safe form of a pathogen that triggers the body to build immunity without causing illness.
White blood cells called lymphocytes produce antibodies and memory cells in response to the antigens in a vaccine.
If the live pathogen later enters the body, memory cells trigger a much faster and stronger secondary response.

lessons.description: How the pulmonary and systemic circuits work together to pump blood through the heart twice per complete circuit.
keyPoints: The left ventricle has a thicker wall than the right ventricle because it pumps blood around the whole body at a higher pressure.
Valves in the heart close to prevent the backflow of blood, ensuring it flows in one direction only.
The right ventricle pumps blood to the lungs, and the left ventricle pumps blood to the rest of the body.
In double circulation, blood passes through the heart twice for each complete circuit of the body.
Returning blood to the heart after the lungs gives it a fresh push at high pressure, delivering oxygen to the body more quickly.
During exercise, the heart beats faster and more strongly to deliver more oxygen to the respiring muscles.

lessons.description: Working out the percentage change in mass of each cylinder, and using a graph to estimate the concentration of the cell sap.
The step-by-step method of choosing and breeding organisms over many generations to strengthen a desired trait.
keyPoints: Humans use selective breeding to pass on desired characteristics, such as high food yield or disease resistance.
Two different characteristics can be combined by crossing varieties and selecting the best offspring over generations.
The selective breeding process involves choosing the best individuals, breeding them, and repeating this with the best offspring over many generations.
Natural selection is a slow process driven by the environment, whereas artificial selection is much faster and driven by humans.
Natural selection maintains variation in a population, while artificial selection reduces it.
Inbreeding increases the chance that offspring will inherit harmful genetic defects.
A lack of variation makes selectively bred populations highly vulnerable to new diseases or environmental changes.

lessons.description: How exchange surfaces are adapted to move substances quickly, including a large surface area and short diffusion distances.
keyPoints: Large multicellular organisms need specialised exchange surfaces because they cannot supply all their cells by diffusion across their outside surface alone.
A large surface area allows more of a substance to diffuse across at the same time.
A thin exchange surface provides a short diffusion distance, making exchange fast.
Maintaining a steep concentration gradient ensures substances keep diffusing in the right direction.
A good blood supply or ventilation helps maintain a steep concentration gradient across the exchange surface.

lessons.description: How random mutations create resistant bacteria, and how natural selection builds them into a resistant strain.
keyPoints: Bacteria can develop a random mutation that makes them resistant to a particular antibiotic.
The antibiotic acts as a selection pressure, killing non-resistant bacteria but allowing resistant ones to survive.
Resistant bacteria reproduce and pass on the resistance allele, quickly building up an antibiotic-resistant strain.

lessons.description: How the four bases pair up across the two strands and hold the double helix together.
keyPoints: DNA is the chemical that makes up genetic material, found in chromosomes in the nucleus.
A DNA molecule is a polymer made of two strands coiled into a double helix.
The four bases in DNA are adenine (A), thymine (T), cytosine (C) and guanine (G).
The two strands are held together by weak hydrogen bonds between paired bases.
Adenine always pairs with thymine, and cytosine always pairs with guanine.
Because bases pair in a fixed way, the sequence of bases on one strand determines the sequence on the other.

lessons.description: How to use a grid to find the possible genotypes and phenotypes of offspring from a genetic cross.
keyPoints: An organism normally carries two alleles for a single gene, inheriting one from each parent.
A homozygous parent produces only one kind of gamete, while a heterozygous parent produces two different kinds.
A Punnett square is a grid used to work out every possible combination of alleles the offspring could inherit.
The ratio of phenotypes from a genetic cross is a prediction of probability, not a guaranteed outcome.
Crossing two heterozygous parents typically produces a 3:1 ratio of the dominant to the recessive characteristic.

lessons.description: The seven life processes that all living things share, and what each one means.
keyPoints: All living organisms share seven life processes, often remembered using the acronym MRS GREN.
Movement is an action by an organism or part of an organism that causes a change of place or position.
Respiration releases the energy needed for an organism's metabolism.
Sensitivity allows organisms to detect and respond to changes in their internal or external environment.
Growth is measured as a permanent increase in an organism's dry mass, ignoring temporary changes in water content.
Reproduction produces new individuals of the same kind so that the species continues.
Excretion removes the waste products of metabolism and any substances the organism has in excess.
Nutrition involves taking in materials used for energy, growth, and development.

lessons.description: How mutations happen spontaneously, and how radiation and certain chemicals can increase the mutation rate.
keyPoints: A mutation is a random change to DNA that produces a new genetic variant.
A mutation can change the sequence of amino acids in a protein, which can alter its shape and stop it working.
Most mutations have no effect on the phenotype.
Mutations happen spontaneously, but ionising radiation and certain chemicals can increase the mutation rate.

lessons.description: How the nephrons filter the blood under high pressure and selectively reabsorb the substances the body needs.
keyPoints: The renal artery brings blood to the kidney, and the renal vein carries filtered blood away.
Urine passes from the kidney down the ureter to the bladder, where it is stored before leaving through the urethra.
Blood is filtered in millions of tiny tube-like structures called nephrons.
A high pressure builds up in the glomerulus because the arteriole entering it is wider than the arteriole leaving it.
High pressure in the glomerulus forces water, glucose, urea and ions into the Bowman's capsule.
Large molecules like proteins and blood cells stay in the blood because they are too large to be filtered out.
All the glucose is selectively reabsorbed back into the blood by active transport.
Sufficient ions and most of the water are reabsorbed, leaving urea, excess water and excess ions to form urine.

lessons.description: How unspecialised cells develop specific structures by switching genes on and off, and when this happens.
keyPoints: Specialised cells have specific structures that adapt them to perform particular functions.
Egg cells contain nutrients for the embryo, a haploid nucleus, and a membrane that changes structure after fertilisation.
Sperm cells have a tail to swim, mitochondria to release energy, and enzymes in the acrosome to digest the egg's outer layer.
Ciliated epithelial cells have cilia that beat to move substances, such as mucus, along the surface of a tissue.
Differentiation is the process where a cell develops specific sub-cellular structures to become specialised.
Most animal cells lose the ability to differentiate early on, but many plant cells can differentiate throughout their lives.
A cell differentiates by switching off most of its genes so it only makes the proteins needed for its specific job.

lessons.description: How a gene is copied into mRNA by RNA polymerase, and how tRNA delivers amino acids to the ribosome.
keyPoints: A gene is a section of DNA that codes for a specific sequence of amino acids to make a protein.
The bases in a gene are read in groups of three, and each triplet codes for a single amino acid.
Once the chain of amino acids is complete, it folds into a unique 3D shape that allows the protein to do its specific job.
Messenger RNA carries a copy of the genetic code from the nucleus out to a ribosome in the cytoplasm.
During transcription, RNA polymerase uses the DNA as a template to build a complementary strand of messenger RNA.
During translation, transfer RNA delivers amino acids to the ribosome by pairing its anticodon with the matching messenger RNA codon.

lessons.description: How phagocytes and lymphocytes protect the body against infection by pathogens.
keyPoints: Red blood cells have a biconcave disc shape and no nucleus to leave more room for oxygen.
Haemoglobin binds to oxygen in the lungs and releases it in the body tissues.
Phagocytes engulf and digest unwelcome microorganisms.
Lymphocytes produce specific antibodies that bind to antigens on pathogens.
Platelets are cell fragments that clump together at a wound to form a clot.
Soluble fibrinogen is converted into an insoluble fibrin mesh that traps blood cells to seal a cut.
Plasma is a liquid that transports dissolved substances and heat around the body.

lessons.description: The structural features of a leaf that help it capture light and make glucose.
keyPoints: The upper epidermis is transparent to let light pass straight through to the photosynthesising cells below.
The palisade mesophyll is packed with chloroplasts and sits near the top of the leaf to capture the most light.
The spongy mesophyll has large air spaces that allow carbon dioxide and oxygen to diffuse easily.
Xylem brings water and mineral ions to the leaf, while phloem carries away the sugars made in photosynthesis.
Leaves are broad and thin to give a large surface area and a short diffusion distance for light and gases.
Stomata are tiny pores on the lower surface of the leaf that let carbon dioxide in and oxygen out.
Guard cells become turgid to open the stomata and flaccid to close them, controlling water loss and gas exchange.

lessons.description: How bacteria and fungi break down dead matter by secreting enzymes, recycling nutrients back into the soil.
keyPoints: Trophic levels are numbered from level 1 upwards, starting with producers.
Producers are plants and algae that capture energy from the Sun to make biomass.
Consumers are animals that get their energy by eating other organisms.
Food chains rarely have more than five levels because energy is lost at each transfer.
Decomposers are bacteria and fungi that feed on dead and waste organic matter.
Decomposers feed by secreting enzymes to break down large molecules into small soluble ones that diffuse into their cells.
By breaking down dead matter, decomposers return nutrients to the soil for producers to use again.

lessons.description: What evolution is, and how the gradual change of a population over time can eventually give rise to new species.
keyPoints: Individuals in a population show genetic variation because they have different combinations of alleles.
Selection pressures such as limited resources, predation and disease mean that not all offspring survive.
Individuals with characteristics that make them better adapted are more likely to survive, reproduce and pass on their alleles.
Evolution is the change in the inherited characteristics of a population over time.
All of today's species evolved from simple life forms that first developed more than three billion years ago.
Two populations become separate species when they can no longer interbreed to produce fertile offspring.

lessons.description: How carbon moves between the atmosphere, living organisms, the soil, and fossil fuels.
keyPoints: The amount of carbon on Earth is fixed, so it must be constantly recycled through the carbon cycle.
Plants and algae remove carbon dioxide from the air during photosynthesis.
Carbon is passed along food chains when animals eat plants or other animals.
Plants, animals, and decomposers return carbon to the atmosphere as carbon dioxide when they respire.
Decomposers break down dead material and release mineral ions back into the soil.
Burning wood and fossil fuels releases stored carbon back into the air as carbon dioxide.
Dead organisms buried without oxygen for millions of years can form fossil fuels, locking carbon away.

lessons.description: How the intercostal muscles and diaphragm change the volume and pressure of the chest to move air in and out.
keyPoints: Air passes through the trachea, bronchi and bronchioles to reach the alveoli.
To breathe in, the intercostal muscles and diaphragm contract to increase the volume of the thorax and lower its pressure.
To breathe out, the intercostal muscles and diaphragm relax to decrease the volume of the thorax and raise its pressure.

lessons.description: How the pancreas responds to high blood glucose by releasing insulin.
keyPoints: Glucose enters the blood from the digestive system and is removed by cells for respiration.
Excess glucose is converted into glycogen and stored in the liver and muscles.
The pancreas constantly monitors the concentration of glucose in the blood.
If blood glucose rises too high, the pancreas secretes the hormone insulin.
Insulin causes the liver and muscles to take in glucose and store it as glycogen.

lessons.description: How changes in environmental factors affect population sizes and where species are found.
keyPoints: Abiotic factors are the non-living parts of an environment, such as light intensity, temperature and soil pH.
Biotic factors are the living parts of an environment, such as food availability, predators and pathogens.
Both abiotic and biotic factors affect the distribution and abundance of organisms in a habitat.
A change in a single environmental factor can have knock-on effects across a whole community.
A drop in light, temperature or carbon dioxide lowers the rate of photosynthesis, which can reduce plant populations.
New predators, pathogens or stronger competitors can drive down the population of a species.

lessons.description: How concentration gradient, temperature, surface area and diffusion distance change how quickly particles spread.
keyPoints: Diffusion is the net movement of particles down a concentration gradient.
Diffusion is a passive process that does not require energy from the cell.
A steeper concentration gradient and a higher temperature both increase the rate of diffusion.
A larger surface area and a shorter diffusion distance both increase the rate of diffusion.
Cell membranes are partially permeable, allowing small molecules to diffuse through but blocking large ones.
Dissolved substances and gases move in and out of cells by diffusing down their concentration gradients.
Oxygen diffuses into cells for respiration, and carbon dioxide diffuses out as a waste product.
Digested food molecules diffuse from the gut into the blood to be absorbed by the body.
Urea diffuses out of cells into the blood plasma to be removed by the kidneys.

lessons.description: The difference between pollen transferring within the same plant and pollen transferring between two different plants.
keyPoints: The stamen is the male part of a flower and produces pollen grains.
The carpel is the female part of a flower and contains the female gametes.
Pollination is the transfer of pollen grains from an anther to a stigma.
Self-pollination transfers pollen to a stigma on the same plant, while cross-pollination involves a different plant of the same species.
Insect-pollinated flowers have brightly coloured petals, scent and nectaries to attract insects.
Wind-pollinated flowers produce large amounts of small, light pollen and have feathery stigmas to catch it.

lessons.description: How the plant hormone auxin controls growth by causing cells to elongate unevenly in roots and shoots.
keyPoints: Shoots grow towards light and away from gravity to absorb more light for photosynthesis.
Roots grow towards gravity and away from light to anchor the plant and reach water.
Auxin is a plant hormone produced in the tips of shoots and roots that causes cells to elongate.
Auxin promotes cell growth in shoots but inhibits cell growth in roots.
Auxin builds up on the shaded side of a shoot, causing it to bend towards the light.
Gravity causes auxin to gather on the lower side of a horizontal root, making it bend downwards.

lessons.description: How animals and plants differ in their cell structures, how they feed, and how they store carbohydrates.
keyPoints: Eukaryotic organisms are made of cells that contain a nucleus.
Prokaryotic organisms are single cells that have no nucleus.
Plants are multicellular organisms that have cellulose cell walls and make their own food by photosynthesis.
Animals are multicellular organisms that have no cell walls and feed by eating other organisms.
Plants store carbohydrates as sucrose or starch, whereas animals store them as glycogen.
Most fungi feed by saprotrophic nutrition, secreting digestive enzymes onto their food outside the body.
Fungi have cell walls made of chitin and bodies usually organised into a mycelium.
Bacteria are microscopic, single-celled organisms with a circular chromosome instead of a nucleus.
Viruses are non-living particles that can only reproduce inside the living cells of a host.

lessons.description: How root hair cells use energy to absorb mineral ions from the soil against a concentration gradient.
keyPoints: Active transport moves particles across a cell membrane against a concentration gradient.
Active transport requires energy transferred by respiration, which is carried by ATP.
Carrier proteins in the cell membrane use energy to move particles across.
Plants use active transport to absorb mineral ions from dilute solutions in the soil into their root hair cells.
Root hair cells have long extensions that give them a large surface area for absorbing water and mineral ions.
Active transport allows animals to absorb nutrients from the gut into the blood when the concentration in the gut is lower.
Cells lining the gut have many mitochondria to provide the energy needed for active transport.
The kidney uses active transport to reabsorb all the glucose from the filtered blood so none is lost in urine.

lessons.description: What male and female sex cells are in animals and plants, and how they carry half the normal genetic information.
keyPoints: Sexual reproduction combines genetic information from two parents to produce genetically different offspring.
Asexual reproduction involves only one parent dividing by mitosis to produce genetically identical clones.
Gametes are sex cells that carry half the normal amount of genetic information.
Male gametes are sperm cells in animals and are carried in pollen grains in plants, while female gametes are egg cells.
At fertilisation, the haploid nucleus of a sperm fuses with the haploid nucleus of an egg to form a diploid zygote.
The zygote divides by mitosis to form a ball of cells called an embryo, which implants into the lining of the uterus.
Human gametes contain 23 chromosomes, while human diploid cells contain 46 chromosomes.

lessons.description: The terms used to describe an organism's genetic make-up and the physical traits it produces.
keyPoints: An organism normally has two alleles of each gene, inheriting one from each parent.
A dominant allele is always expressed when present.
A recessive allele is only expressed when no dominant allele is present.
An organism's genotype is its combination of alleles, and its phenotype is the characteristics they produce.
An organism is homozygous if its two alleles for a gene are the same, and heterozygous if they are different.
Two organisms can have different genotypes but the same phenotype if one is homozygous dominant and the other is heterozygous.
In codominance, neither allele is recessive, so both are expressed in the phenotype at the same time.

lessons.description: The five key sub-cellular structures that make up an animal cell, and what each one does.
keyPoints: Eukaryotic cells have a nucleus and membrane-bound sub-cellular structures, while prokaryotic cells are smaller and have no nucleus.
Animal cells contain a nucleus, cytoplasm, cell membrane, mitochondria and ribosomes.
Plant cells have all the structures of an animal cell, plus a cellulose cell wall, a permanent vacuole and chloroplasts.
Bacterial cells are prokaryotic, so their genetic material is a single circular loop of DNA floating freely in the cytoplasm.
Bacterial cells may also contain small rings of DNA called plasmids, which can carry extra genes.
Fungal cells are eukaryotic and have a cell wall made of chitin instead of cellulose.
Some fungi are single-celled, while others have a body made of a mycelium network built from thread-like hyphae.

lessons.description: What plants and animals compete for, and the difference between interspecific and intraspecific competition.
keyPoints: An ecosystem is the interaction of a community of living organisms with the non-living parts of their environment.
Plants compete for light, space, water and mineral ions.
Animals compete for food, water, territory and mates.
Intraspecific competition is more intense than interspecific competition because members of the same species need the exact same resources.
In a community, a change to one species can cause knock-on effects that impact many other species.

lessons.description: What the genome is, what it contains, and why it is the same in nearly every cell.
keyPoints: Genetic information is stored in DNA, which is coiled up tightly to form chromosomes.
In body cells, chromosomes are normally found in pairs, with one from each parent.
A gene is a section of DNA on a chromosome that codes for a particular protein.
Genes control the inherited characteristics of an organism by setting which proteins the cell makes.
The genome is the entire genetic material of an organism.
Nearly every cell in an organism contains a full copy of its genome.

lessons.description: How the eye automatically adjusts the size of the pupil to control the amount of light reaching the retina.
keyPoints: The cornea refracts light as it enters the eye and does most of the focusing.
The lens fine-tunes the focusing to bring light to a sharp focus on the retina.
The retina contains rod cells for vision in dim light and cone cells for colour vision.
The optic nerve carries electrical impulses from the retina to the brain.
The iris reflex automatically changes the size of the pupil to control how much light enters the eye.
In bright light, the circular muscles contract and the radial muscles relax to make the pupil smaller.
In dim light, the radial muscles contract and the circular muscles relax to make the pupil wider.

lessons.description: How warming speeds up enzyme reactions, and why extreme heat denatures them and stops them working.
keyPoints: Enzymes are biological catalysts that speed up reactions without being used up.
An enzyme has a specifically shaped active site that only fits a complementary substrate.
As temperature rises towards the optimum, enzyme reactions speed up because the molecules meet and react more often.
Above the optimum temperature, bonds break and the enzyme permanently denatures.
Enzymes have an optimum pH, and extreme acidity or alkalinity will denature them.

lessons.description: How the walls, lumens and valves of arteries and veins are adapted to the pressure of the blood they carry.
keyPoints: Blood leaves the heart through arteries, passes through capillaries in the tissues, and returns to the heart through veins.
Arteries carry blood away from the heart at high pressure, so they have thick walls with muscle and elastic fibres.
Veins carry blood back to the heart at lower pressure, so they have wide lumens and one-way valves to prevent backflow.
Capillaries have very thin walls and form extensive networks to exchange substances between the blood and the tissues.
The hepatic artery brings oxygenated blood to the liver, and the hepatic vein carries blood away.
The hepatic portal vein brings blood containing the products of digestion from the digestive system to the liver.

lessons.description: The structural features of the alveoli that make the diffusion of gases as fast as possible.
keyPoints: Oxygen diffuses from the air in the alveoli into the blood, and carbon dioxide diffuses from the blood into the alveoli.
Pleural fluid reduces friction as the lungs move against the inside of the chest during breathing.
Alveoli have walls that are only one cell thick to provide a very short diffusion path for gases.
A huge number of alveoli provides a large surface area so more gas can diffuse at the same time.
A constant blood supply and good ventilation keep the concentration gradients steep for fast diffusion.
